opus-5.5.text:
I think agent tasks actually require quite a lot of reasoning, though maybe not in the way people usually picture it.

When people say "reasoning," they often think of math competitions or hard logic puzzles, where the model thinks for a long time and finally produces one answer. Agent tasks are different. The reasoning is spread across many steps. At each step the model has to understand where it is, what information it has, what is still missing, and which action to take next. Then the environment gives feedback, and it has to update its plan. So it's less like solving one very hard problem and more like making a long sequence of moderately hard decisions, where errors compound.

That's why I think long-horizon reasoning matters so much. If each step is 95% correct, after twenty or thirty steps the success rate collapses. So a model needs more than raw intelligence on a single step. It needs to be robust over long trajectories. It should notice when it has made a mistake, backtrack, try another path, and not get stuck in a loop. That self-correction ability is a very important part of reasoning for agents.

There's also a tight coupling between reasoning and tool use. A good agent shouldn't try to figure everything out in its head. It should know when to search, when to run code, when to read a file, and when to stop and think. Good reasoning includes deciding what you don't know and how to find it out efficiently. In a sense, the model's thinking and its actions become interleaved, rather than "think first, then act."

So my view is that reasoning and agentic capability aren't two separate things. Agent tasks are where reasoning gets tested most realistically, because the problem isn't neatly packaged for you. And training on these kinds of long, interactive tasks, especially with reinforcement learning on real outcomes, also feeds back into the model's general reasoning. I think that's one of the most important directions right now: scaling the length and complexity of the tasks a model can reliably complete on its own.

r001.rationale: The response describes agent tasks as sequences of moderately hard decisions, but never states that choosing the next action does not require thousands of tokens of deliberation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think reasoning is actually the foundation of agent capability, not something separate from it. When people talk about agents, they often imagine the hard part is tool calling or the scaffolding around the model, but in our experience the bottleneck almost always comes back to whether the model can think correctly over a long horizon.

An agent task is really a long chain of decisions. At each step the model has to understand the current state, figure out what it doesn't know yet, decide which action gets it closer to the goal, and then interpret the result, which is often noisy or unexpected. If the reasoning is weak at any one step, errors compound. A task that takes fifty or a hundred steps will fail even if the per-step accuracy looks pretty good. So the demand on reasoning is actually much higher for agents than for a single-turn question, because you need consistency across the whole trajectory, not just a correct answer at the end.

There's also a second kind of reasoning that matters, which I'd call reflection or self-correction. When a tool returns an error or the environment doesn't behave as expected, the model has to recognize that its plan was wrong and revise it, rather than keep pushing in the same direction. That's quite close to what reinforcement learning with long-horizon reward teaches the model. Our view with Kimi has been that if you first make the model strong at reasoning, then agentic ability emerges fairly naturally when you give it tools and the right training signal. Doing it the other way around, building elaborate agent frameworks on top of a model that can't really think, tends to hit a ceiling very quickly.

So my short answer is: a lot. Probably more than people assume. The agent is really just reasoning extended over time and connected to the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes agent tasks as requiring sustained, high reasoning across many steps, but does not state that choosing the next action in some tasks needs fewer than thousands of tokens of deliberation.

astra-6.text:
I think agent tasks can require quite a lot of reasoning, but it depends on the task. If you’re following a fixed workflow—opening a page, finding a field, entering some information—the reasoning requirement may be relatively modest. But if the goal is open-ended, you have to decide what to do, interpret the results, and revise your plan when something doesn’t work. That’s much more demanding.

What makes agents interesting is that reasoning happens throughout the interaction. You take an action, get new information, and then reason again. So it’s not just about producing a good plan at the beginning. It’s about knowing whether you’re making progress and what to do next.

And reasoning alone isn’t enough. You also need reliable tool use and the ability to keep track of the task over many steps. A model can be very good at solving an isolated problem and still struggle to complete a long task because small mistakes accumulate.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended tasks require deciding what to do next, but does not state that this can be done without thousands of tokens of deliberation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agent tasks can require quite a lot of reasoning, but it depends on the task. If you’re following a clear procedure, the main challenge may be executing reliably. If the goal is open-ended, you need to break it down, decide which tools to use, interpret the results, and adjust your plan when something doesn’t work.

What makes this difficult is that you’re reasoning over a sequence of actions. A decision that looks reasonable locally might take you in the wrong direction, and you may only discover that several steps later. So the agent needs to keep track of the goal and evaluate its own progress.

But reasoning alone isn’t enough. You also need reliable tool use and good feedback from the environment. I’d think of reasoning as one essential part of the whole system.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning demands vary by task and that clear procedures may mainly require reliable execution, but it does not state that choosing the next action in some tasks needs fewer than thousands of tokens of deliberation.
